note: claude-opus-5-5、入力 2940 / 出力 2856 トークン

data.interpretation: From period 5 the KPI shifts emphasis. On-time delivery still matters, but the leading concern ('but ... no single company should gain or lose') is fairness between companies under the road rules. 'Gain or lose' is best measured by company utility (on-time deliveries minus sanctions), because road rules affect both deliveries and sanctions. 'Still matters' reads as a floor and a watched goal, not the main goal. Because orders fall in the quiet season, absolute counts shrink, so guards should use rates rather than counts. The KPI can be read in different ways, so I offer three evaluation methods for the human to choose from.

options.label: Fairness of utility first, on-time as a floor

goals.text: Decrease the gap between the best and worst company's utility (on-time deliveries minus sanctions).
Watch that the worst company's on-time rate does not fall.
Watch that town-wide on-time deliveries do not fall.
Watch that total sanctions do not rise, so the gap does not narrow simply by penalising everyone.

guards.text: Every company keeps at least a 70% on-time rate (the provisional floor carried over from K1).

options.note: Closest to 'gain or lose'. Utility covers both deliveries and penalties, and both depend on road rules. Risk: the gap can shrink by levelling down, which is why the monitored goals and the floor are included.

options.label: Fairness of on-time rate first

goals.text: Decrease the gap between the best and worst company's on-time rate.
Watch that the utility gap does not widen.
Watch that town-wide on-time deliveries do not fall.

guards.text: Every company keeps at least a 70% on-time rate.

options.note: Measures fairness as the service customers receive, ignoring sanctions. A rate is less sensitive to falling order volume than counts are. However, it misses gains or losses that come from sanctions.

options.label: On-time deliveries first, fairness as hard limits

goals.text: Watch that the utility gap does not widen.
Watch that late deliveries do not rise.

guards.text: Company on-time rates differ by at most 10 percentage points.
Every company keeps at least a 70% on-time rate.

options.note: Keeps the previous main goal and treats fairness only as limits. This fits the wording 'still matters' less well, and in a quiet season the gains in absolute counts will be small.

concerns: The KPI says no company should gain or lose 'because of how the road is used', but utility_gap and on_time_rate_gap measure total differences between companies. Those differences also reflect each company's own demand and fleet use, so the gap metrics are only proxies for the rule-caused effect.

Narrowing a gap can be achieved by making the best company worse off rather than helping the worst one. This would meet the metric but break 'no single company should ... lose'. Monitored goals and a floor reduce this risk but do not remove it.
On-time delivery and fairness can conflict. A rule that raises town-wide on-time deliveries may shift utility between companies, as D1 did when C's utility fell from 28.8 to 19.0.

Orders fall in the quiet season, so count-based figures (on_time_deliveries, late_deliveries, sanction_total) are not comparable with periods 1–4. The 0.7 floor was explicitly provisional in K1, and measured worst-company rates have been around 0.98, so the floor may be too loose to protect anyone.

revisit.why: K1's reading (town-wide on-time deliveries as the main goal) is replaced by a KPI that puts fairness between companies first. Its 0.7 floor was provisional and should be reset in light of measured rates and the quiet season.

D1 was adopted against B's and C's votes even though it cut C's utility from 28.8 to 19.0. Under the new KPI, a company losing utility because of a road rule is exactly what should be avoided. The human also asked for C's utility and road violations to be re-measured, so v2 block_k 3 → 2 should be re-evaluated against utility_gap.
